question: A 70-year-old woman presents to her primary care doctor complaining of left knee pain. She states that she has noticed this more during the past several months after a fall at home. Previously, she was without pain and has no history of trauma to her knees. The patient states that the majority of her pain starts in the afternoon after she has been active for some time, and that the pain resolves with rest and over-the-counter analgesics. Aside from the left knee, she has no other symptoms and no other joint findings. On exam, her temperature is 98.8°F (37.1°C), blood pressure is 124/76 mmHg, pulse is 70/min, and respirations are 12/min. The patient has no limitations in her range of motion and no changes in strength on motor testing. However, there is tenderness along the medial joint line. What finding is most likely seen in this patient?
reasoning_chain: CHAIN: "Left knee pain after fall" -> "Pain starts in the afternoon after activity" -> "Pain resolves with rest and analgesics" -> "Tenderness along the medial joint line" -> "Possible increased synovial fluid" -> 70%

CHAIN: "Left knee pain after fall" -> "Pain starts in the afternoon after activity" -> "Pain resolves with rest and analgesics" -> "Tenderness along the medial joint line" -> "No limitations in range of motion or strength" -> "Unlikely to have joint pannus" -> 80%

analysis: The patient's presentation of knee pain that worsens with activity, improves with rest, and is associated with tenderness along the medial joint line is suggestive of osteoarthritis. Heberden nodes are bony enlargements seen at the distal interphalangeal joints in osteoarthritis of the hands, not the knee. Increased synovial fluid, joint pannus, and marginal sclerosis are more commonly associated with inflammatory arthritis like rheumatoid arthritis, which is less likely in this patient based on the clinical presentation.
